segments.text: Euclid's Elements, Book One, Proposition Sixteen. In any triangle, if one side is extended, the exterior angle is greater than either opposite interior angle. Given triangle A B C with side B C extended to point D, we prove that exterior angle A C D is greater than either opposite interior angle B A C or C B A.

segments.text: Using Proposition Ten, bisect segment A C at point E so that A E equals E C. Join segment B E and extend it to F, cutting off E F equal to B E by Proposition Three. Then join segment F C, and extend segment A C through to point G.

segments.text: By Proposition Fifteen, vertical angles A E B and F E C are equal. Since sides A E and E B equal sides C E and E F, Proposition Four proves that triangles A B E and C F E are congruent, so angle B A E equals angle E C F. Because the whole exterior angle E C D is greater than its part E C F, exterior angle A C D is greater than angle B A C. Similarly, bisecting B C proves that vertical angle B C G, and therefore angle A C D, is also greater than angle C B A, as was required to prove.
